name: Katiang Palaung of Hsipaw
confidence_why: Buakaw, Rattanapitak and Deepadung 2018 describe the Katiang presyllable as unstressed with the main syllable carrying the stress, Weymuth 2022 independently reports an iambic structure for Rumai of Nam Hkam in which prefixes are never stressed and the second word of a compound is stressed, and Chen, Wang and Lai 1986 and Dai and Liu 1997 describe the same weakened presyllables in the Chinese De'ang and Guangka Rumai varieties, with no source disagreeing.

catalog_locator: Buakaw et al. 2018 pp.4-6: sec. 2.1 'Words' (p.4), sec. 2.1.2 'Polysyllabic words' (p.5), sec. 2.2 'Syllable structure' (p.6). Cross-checks: Dai & Liu 1997 pp.92-93, 96-97; Chen et al. 1986 pp.16, 18, 108.
catalog_quote: p.4: "A word in Katiang is either monosyllabic or polysyllabic. Monosyllabic words consist of a major syllable and may be an open or closed syllable. Polysyllabic words are words that consist of a presyllable and a major syllable." p.5: "As for Katiang polysyllabic words, there are two types, namely, a sesquisyllabic word and a compound word. The sesquisyllable consists of one main syllable preceded by a presyllable. Phonologically, presyllable is an unstressed syllable the vowel of which is limited to low central vowel /a/, as shown in Table 2." [Table 2: kafaŋ 'ash', sanăm 'year', saŋɛh 'delicious', ʔaɡaw 'rice (pounded rice)', ʔarok 'frog', kaʔaŋ 'bone'] p.6: "The minor syllable of Katiang is an unstressed syllable, namely a presyllable, which is preceded by the major syllable. The structure of a presyllable is an initial consonant followed by the vowel /a/- CV. The vowel /a/ in a presyllable is pronounced as a schwa [ə]. Phonemes /p-, k-, kh-, c-, s-, ŋ-, n-, Ɂ-/ are found in the initial consonant position of a presyllable, as shown in Table 6."
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: All three quoted passages are verbatim on the saved files. (1), text p.5 sec. 2.1.2: "The sesquisyllable consists of one main syllable preceded by a presyllable. Phonologically, presyllable is an unstressed syllable the vowel of which is limited to low central vowel /a/"; p.6 sec. 2.2: "The minor syllable of Katiang is an unstressed syllable, namely a presyllable.. The vowel /a/ in a presyllable is pronounced as a schwa [ə]." The word "tone" never occurs in the 16-page phonology (consonants, vowels, finals, clusters described in full), so the description is non-tonal. (2) Chen, Wang & Lai 1986 p.18, checked on the page scan jianzhi_pages/printed page 18, sec. 2 前加音节 note (2)): the sentence…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Words are monosyllables or sesquisyllables (presyllable + major syllable). Stress falls on the major syllable, which is the final syllable of the word; the presyllable is unstressed, its vowel reduced to schwa (Katiang) or 'light/weakened, indistinct, unstable' (Bulei). In Rumai proper (Guangka, Ruili) the major syllable carries one of three fixed lexical tones while the weakened first syllable has no clear tone.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for stress. Compound words (two major syllables) are not assigned a stress pattern by any source. Dai & Liu 1997: in Guangka the tone of the first syllable of a disyllable varies with the tone of the second; some words lack a fixed tone.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms: the sesquisyllabic word = (presyllable) + major syllable; only the major (final) syllable is stressed. The three sources cover three different varieties filed under rbb/ruma1248: Buakaw et al. 2018 = Katiang of Hsipaw (non-tonal description); Chen et al. 1986 p.18 = Yunqian/Bulei, Luxi (no lexical tone, p.16); Dai & Liu 1997 = Guangka, Ruili = Rumai proper, which is tonal (three fixed tones; the presyllable is 'weakened' and its tone unclear; p.93) and Chen et al. 1986 p.108 also gives the Rumai dialect two tones (55, 51). If the catalog wants the Rumai-proper variety, the reading would be tone language with a stress statement with the same major-syllable prominence; the Katiang/Bulei statements are the only ones that use the word stress/轻读.
new_statements.identity_note: ruma1248 / ISO rbb lumps several varieties. The deciding English statement (Buakaw et al. 2018, Glottolog phonology ref for ruma1248) describes Katiang of Hsipaw, which its authors place between the Dehong Palaung group (Liang, Pule, Rumai) and the Darang group, 'closer to Darang' — not Rumai of Namhkam proper. Chen, Wang & Lai 1986 p.18 describes the Yunqian/Bulei 布雷 dialect (Luxi, Yunnan), which Glottolog files under ruma1248 (ref 688923) but which Deepadung et al. 2015 group with Pule/Pale [pce]; its Rumai 汝买 dialect sketch (p.108) and Dai & Liu 1997 (Guangka, Ruili) describe Rumai proper in China, which is tonal (2-3 tones). Rumai of Nam Hkam/Man Ton (Myanmar, Weymuth's variety, the bulk of speakers) has no accessible phonological description yet (Weymuth 2022 not opened).

new_statements.quote: p.14: "As Rumai has an iambic structure, only the second word in a compound would be stressed." p.31: "In Rumai however, some morphemes are not in free occurrence, but they are verbal or nominal affixes. These morphemes are never stressed and some of them show phonetic features, which don't occur with independent morphemes." p.13: "How prominent the tone and voice distinctions are in colloquial speech is not yet clear. More investigation will show whether tones and voice are distinctive features in Rumai."

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's rule 01 (final stress in the sesquisyllable, presyllable unstressed, from Buakaw et al. 2018 on Katiang): Weymuth generalizes it as an iambic structure in which pre-syllables/affixes are never stressed and the second word of a compound carries the stress. Adds: (a) domain extends to compounds; (b) Rumai of Nam Hkam has script-marked tone/voice contrasts of uncertain phonemic status, which Buakaw et al. do not report for Katiang. Describes Rumai proper (Nam Hkam), not Katiang of Hsipaw.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No dedicated stress section; stress is mentioned in passing. Rumai words are mostly monosyllabic, with sesquisyllabic (reduced pre-syllable + main syllable) and disyllabic words (p.13). The language has an 'iambic structure': prominence falls on the last element, so in a compound only the second word is stressed (p.14), and affixes (mostly prefixes, incl. reduced pre-syllables such as kʰə-) are never stressed (p.31, p.62). The Palaung script also marks five tone/voice categories (high, falling, middle, low/breathy, creaky; p.12), but the author says it is not yet clear whether tone and voice are distinctive (p.13).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. The author notes that tones of second elements are lost in some disyllabic words like kʰaj.hmeɛ 'when' and that irrealis-pronoun mergers lose the pronoun's falling tone (p.13, p.60 fn.5); compound status of two-word sequences (sʌw kətâːj 'fox') is to be settled by intonation studies (p.14).
new_statements.identity_note: Weymuth 2022 describes Rumai Palaung (ISO rbb) of Nam Hkam township, northern Shan State, Myanmar (main consultant from Man Sat village; other consultants recorded in Mandalay and Lashio, 2013-2020), which is the nominal language of glottocode ruma1248. The catalog record for ruma1248 is instead based on Buakaw et al. 2018's Katiang Palaung of Hsipaw, which those authors place between the Dehong (Liang/Pule/Rumai) group and the Darang group, 'closer to Darang'; so the catalog's entry name and its source variety are not Rumai of Nam Hkam proper, although both show the same unstressed-presyllable/final-prominence pattern.

tone_statements.citation: Weymuth, Rachel. 2016. Palaung language and identity. The Newsletter (International Institute for Asian Studies, Leiden) 75 (Autumn 2016): 39.
tone_statements.quote: The sound systems of the languages also differ. Rumai, for example, appears to have a falling tone, at least in some dialects. The other Palaung varieties, like most of the Austroasiatic languages generally, are not tonal.
tone_statements.locator: The Newsletter (IIAS) no. 75, Autumn 2016, p. 39, section 'Language variation', end of the paragraph that follows the 'this is not my house' examples (Samlong / Rumai / Rucing)
tone_statements.summary: Rumai: a (contrastive?) falling tone in some dialects, hedged; other Palaung non-tonal.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement on stress: Weymuth 2022 (Rumai of Nam Hkam: iambic structure, affixes/pre-syllables never stressed, second word of a compound stressed) agrees with Buakaw et al. 2018 (Katiang of Hsipaw: presyllable unstressed, main syllable stressed) and with Chen et al. 1986 (presyllable vowel always weakened). The sources differ on tone, which is a matter of variety rather than stress: Buakaw et al. 2018 mention no tone for Katiang; Chen et al. 1986 give two tones (55, 51) for the Rumai dialect in China; Dai & Liu 1997 give three tones for Guangka Rumai; Weymuth 2022 lists five script-marked tone/voice categories for Nam Hkam Rumai and leaves their phonemic status open.

sources.note: Rumai proper (Guangka village, Mengxiu, Ruili). p.92: 'Guangka has three tones; almost every syllable has a fixed tone, and there are many tonal minimal pairs.' p.93: 'Guangka has a 31 tone. This tone only appears in the first (weakened) syllable of polysyllabic words, and in borrowings from Chinese. When the weakened syllable of a polysyllabic word serves as a prefix, the tone is not clear.' p.99: Chayeqing (Rumai) has high level and high falling tones; Yunqian (Bulei) and Xiaochanggou (Liang) have no tones. The word 'stress' is never used.

sources.note: Base variety Yunqian 允欠, Luxi = Bulei dialect (pp.4-5). p.18: '一般音节中的元音是固定的，清晰的，不是轻读的，而前加音节中的元音，始终是以轻读、弱化形式出现，含糊不清，很不稳定。' (main-syllable vowel fixed/clear/not light; presyllable vowel always light and weakened). p.7: presyllables k, t, s 'carry a weakened vowel'. p.16: Bulei 'has no tones (字调)'; short-vowel syllables read high-falling, long-vowel lower-falling in slow speech. p.101: dialects Bulei / Rumai 汝买 (Longchuan, Ruili) / Liang. p.108 (Rumai dialect sketch): '汝买话不仅有元音长短的区别，而且还有声调的区分…只分高平调〔55〕和全降调〔51〕两个调' (Rumai has two tones). No 重音 (stress) statement anywhere.

sources.note: Not opened (print only). Second-hand only (zh-Wikipedia 'De'ang yu' article citing this book): Liu Yan 2006 records three De'ang varieties - Guangka village, Mengxiu, Ruili (autonym ru55 mai412, i.e. Rumai) 'has tone'; Mengdan, Santaishan, Luxi (autonym ʔaŋ) 'no tone'; Guanshuang, Mengman, Xishuangbanna (ar31 vaʔ13) 'has tone'. No tone values or inventory for Guangka were seen; that the book restates or extends the Dai & Liu 1997 three-tone analysis is an inference from authorship, not verified.

tone.summary: Guangka Rumai tonal (3 tones per Dai & Liu 1997); Mengdan De'ang toneless.
